title: United States v. Midwest Oil Company
lead: Before Congress changed the oil-land system, President Taft withdrew public acreage from new claims. Later entrants drilled on withdrawn Wyoming land, forcing a dispute over whether established administrative practice could imply congressional authority.

actors.name: President William Howard Taft
actors.role: Directed the September 27, 1909 temporary petroleum withdrawal.

actors.name: Geological Survey director and Secretary of the Interior
actors.role: Recommended and approved retention of remaining petroleum lands pending legislation.

actors.name: William T. Henshaw and fellow entrants
actors.role: Entered withdrawn Wyoming land in March 1910 and later assigned their interests.

actors.name: Midwest Oil Company and other appellees
actors.role: Assignees who possessed the land and extracted oil; defendants in the government’s equity suit.

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Sought recovery of land and an accounting for allegedly unlawful extraction.

proceedings: Federal District Court for Wyoming sustained defendants’ demurrer and dismissed the government’s equity bill.
Eighth Circuit certified questions without deciding the merits; Supreme Court called for the full record and heard argument and reargument.
Supreme Court on February 23, 1915 remanded with directions that the district-court dismissal be reversed, sustaining the withdrawal by a 5–3 vote.
limits: The case did not award a final accounting or determine extracted quantities. The majority reserved presidential power as an original question without the historical practice and denied that executive action alone creates authority. The controlling withdrawal was September 27, 1909, distinct from the July 2, 1910 reaffirmation.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Open oil lands create a race toward private acquisition
sections.cue: What problem led officials to seek temporary retention?
paragraphs: Congress’s February 11, 1897 statute permitted qualified persons to acquire petroleum and mineral-oil lands under placer-mining laws. Revised Statutes §§ 2319 and 2329 formed the broader system opening valuable mineral deposits to exploration and purchase. Oil could drain beneath neighboring parcels into competing wells, encouraging rapid extraction, while private acquisitions depleted public reserves. Officials feared that the government would lose inexpensive naval fuel and later buy oil that it had once owned.

On September 17, 1909, the Geological Survey’s director warned the Interior Secretary that remaining public petroleum lands might soon leave government control and recommended suspending new claims pending legislation. The Secretary agreed. On September 27, under President Taft’s direction, the department issued Temporary Petroleum Withdrawal No. 5. It barred new location, settlement, selection, filing, entry, or disposal under mineral and nonmineral land laws in listed areas while Congress considered petroleum legislation. Existing valid claims could proceed after field investigation and examination.

The listed California and Wyoming areas totaled 3,041,000 acres, but the order reached only public land within them; the report did not establish the actual affected public acreage. As the later dissent emphasized, earlier California restrictions had allowed mining locations, and this directive closed that remaining path. The Wyoming tracts were not identified as prospective naval supply: their withdrawal sought a different statutory disposal system, complicating reliance on naval needs alone.

sources.pinpoint: Land regime and withdrawal; 236 U.S. at 466–67, 484–88

sections.title: Henshaw enters after withdrawal, and Congress later legislates
sections.cue: What had happened before the assignees asserted their rights?
paragraphs: On March 27, 1910, William T. Henshaw and others entered a quarter section of withdrawn Wyoming land. They explored, drilled, discovered oil, and assigned their interests to Midwest Oil and the other eventual appellees, who possessed the land and extracted petroleum. A location certificate was filed May 4. Every step followed the September withdrawal, so the entrants had no prewithdrawal private claim for the order to respect.

On June 25, 1910, Congress expressly authorized temporary withdrawals. The law came after both the executive order and the attempted location. It directed that it neither recognize, abridge, nor enlarge claims begun on oil or gas lands after earlier withdrawals, preserving the contest over those claims. Taft had requested express authority and ratification; a House bill included ratification, but Congress ultimately omitted resolution of disputed public and private rights. The dissent would also discuss Taft’s separate July 2 reaffirmation. Neither that reaffirmation nor the later statute should be confused with the controlling September 1909 order.

sections.title: The government’s recovery suit is dismissed on demurrer
sections.cue: Which court actually entered the judgment under review?
paragraphs: The United States sued in equity to recover the land and obtain an accounting for 50,000 barrels it alleged had been unlawfully extracted. The federal District Court for Wyoming sustained the defendants’ demurrer and dismissed the bill. That posture made the withdrawal’s legal validity central; it did not establish an adjudicated quantity of extracted oil.

The Eighth Circuit certified questions without deciding the merits. The Supreme Court called for the entire record and, after argument and reargument, addressed the controlling validity question. There was no substantive Eighth Circuit ruling for it to reverse.

The government invoked presidential administration of the public domain, naval fuel needs, executive authority, and congressional tacit consent. The oil interests answered that Congress had affirmatively opened these lands and that the President had no dispensing power to suspend the statute while seeking a preferred policy. They also relied on Taft’s request for ratification and Congress’s prospective rather than retroactive legislation.

sources.pinpoint: Proceedings and competing positions; 236 U.S. at 461–69, 483

sections.title: Lamar treats informed congressional acquiescence as implied authority
sections.cue: Why was the history more than evidence that Presidents had acted before?
paragraphs: Justice Lamar began with roughly eighty years of withdrawals of mineral and nonmineral land affecting millions of acres. Excluding special statutory authorizations, the Court counted 99 orders establishing or expanding Indian reservations, 109 military reservations or related facilities, and 44 bird reserves before 1910. In its reading, these 252 useful public reservations lacked specific authorization and had repeatedly been accepted rather than repudiated by Congress. The documentary footnote supported that historical account, which the dissent contested.

Before a claimant initiated a legally protected interest, the disposal laws did not create an enforceable private right in a particular parcel. Holding unappropriated property therefore preserved public ownership without defeating an existing private right. Congress could disaffirm withdrawals, and executive familiarity with local conditions made temporary retention useful while Congress deliberated. Grisar v. McDowell and government law officers’ opinions had recognized the practice.

Drawing on Stuart v. Laird and practical-construction decisions, Lamar treated longstanding arrangements as interpretive evidence even when their validity was disputed. Practice itself could not manufacture power. Rather, Congress’s knowledge and acquiescence supported presumed consent or recognized administrative authority. The majority expressly reserved whether a President would have such power as an original question before the practice existed.

sources.pinpoint: Long practice and implied consent; 236 U.S. at 469–74 & n.1

sections.title: The government’s role as landowner supports its agent’s protective action
sections.cue: Why did awaiting legislation not necessarily invalidate withdrawal?
paragraphs: Congress acted as proprietor of public land as well as legislator under Article IV, § 3. General disposal directions could meet changed conditions requiring an agent temporarily to retain property. An owner’s authorization need not invariably be express. Lamar compared implied grazing and mining licenses: if informed congressional acquiescence could support private privileges, it could also support an agent’s preservation of the owner’s interests. He distinguished improper withdrawals enlarging a railroad’s private statutory grant.

The oil interests tried to separate reservations for public uses from withdrawals merely awaiting legislation. The majority saw temporary withholding as a lesser protective step with the same effect on prospective claimants. The Des Moines River cases provided a direct analogy: land was held while officials and Congress disputed Iowa’s grant, and later settlers acquired no contrary rights. Lamar regarded those withdrawals as valid from the outset, not void orders later cured to the detriment of intervening settlers.

Other examples involved islands, isolated tracts, proposed forests, phosphate, oil, coal, and park lands. Sometimes legislation followed and sometimes it did not; the absence of a later Act did not itself nullify a protective order. The size and duration of withdrawals and Congress’s opportunity to object mattered.

In 1902 the Senate specifically demanded a list of administrative withdrawals and their asserted legal basis. Interior responded with detailed examples and a claimed longstanding power to prevent fraud, aid administration, and support pending legislation when needed. The majority described 92 orders for useful nonstatutory purposes. Congress’s informed failure to repudiate that position supported continuation until it revoked the authority.

sources.pinpoint: Proprietary role and temporary withdrawals; 236 U.S. at 473–81

sections.title: The 1910 savings language leaves earlier rights to earlier law
sections.cue: Why did Lamar conclude ratification was unnecessary?
paragraphs: The majority read the later statute as neither destroying a valid intervening claim nor validating a location already ineffective under a lawful withdrawal. Rights therefore depended on law when the September 1909 order issued. Although Taft had acknowledged doubts and requested ratification, Congress chose not to resolve the contested existing rights; some senators believed he already possessed broader withdrawal power.

For Lamar, the 1910 law prospectively clarified and restricted authority without repudiating prior valid withdrawals. Existing practice and implied congressional consent already authorized this order, making retroactive ratification unnecessary. The entrants consequently acquired no rights through later entry while the valid withdrawal remained operative.

sections.title: Day disputes the analogy and reads omitted ratification against authority
sections.cue: Why did the dissent think this order displaced Congress’s policy?
paragraphs: Justice Day, joined by Justices McKenna and Van Devanter, accepted that express or sufficiently clear implied congressional authority could support withdrawals. He also accepted holding lands for congressionally selected public uses or while resolving ambiguous grants. His objection was that Article IV placed property control in Congress, and presidential execution did not permit suspending an unambiguous disposal law to await a preferred replacement.

Day reread the precedents. Wilcox v. Jackson involved congressionally authorized military, trading-house, and lighthouse uses with statutory reservation exceptions. Grisar involved legislative recognition and appropriations. The Des Moines cases preserved an existing disputed grant, and later continuation protected settlers claiming under Iowa while adjustment was considered. These examples implemented existing policy rather than replaced it. His extended documentary footnote challenged whether all asserted precedents really lacked antecedent authority.

Railroad-grant cases invalidating withdrawals illustrated the boundary: executive action could not defeat Congress’s policy protecting lawful settlers. Implied authority had to amount to congressional authorization, not merely an undifferentiated history of executive conduct. The Wyoming withdrawal sought new legislative policy, and conservation value could not supply missing power.

Day also read 1910 differently. Congress omitted requested ratification, provided restricted future authority, preserved contested claims, and protected specified existing settlements and diligent exploration. That was not the unrestricted prior directive. He thought withholding ratification defeated implied consent and that the July 2 reaffirmation could not cure the original defect. He would leave dismissal intact rather than expand executive authority because another land policy seemed beneficial.

sections.title: The withdrawal survives, but the accounting remains for further proceedings
sections.cue: What exactly did the Supreme Court direct?
paragraphs: On February 23, 1915, the Court sustained the September 27, 1909 withdrawal by a 5–3 vote. Justice McReynolds did not participate. It remanded to the District Court for Wyoming with directions that the decree dismissing the government’s bill be reversed. The judgment reopened the government’s suit; it did not award a final accounting or establish how much oil had been taken.

The holding rested on practice known to Congress, congressional ability to disaffirm it, a proprietary administrative relationship, and absence of preexisting private rights. It did not announce a general presidential power to suspend statutes whenever another policy appeared better. The majority and dissent differed over the historical evidence and the inference from the 1910 law; the source supplies no later accounting outcome.
